doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: A restless creative mind and changing how he breathes
summary: Griffin says his mind is always creating, which led to multiphonics, and that late in life he switched from diaphragmatic to chest breathing.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Would you say your mind is almost always occupied with creating something, whether it’s thinking about music or thinking about a blank canvas. Are you preoccupied with that kind of forward thinking?

I am. And you hit on an area that most people don’t even ask me — I’m like that even when I’m sitting, if I don’t — you know people — just relaxing — I’m either playing chess on my phone or some kind of puzzle or something. My mind is always going, you know like thinking of something creative. And that’s how I discovered the multiphonics in the stuff that I play. Because I always look at something and say there’s a different way of doing it. And I haven’t been as courageous as I lately have about trying the different ways of doing it. Because I was telling my son, we talked — see every coin has two sides, a head and a tail. Every situation that you deal with has a left and a right, a hot and a cold, good and a bad you know. And it’s just — so some people look, they stay under only just the hot side and never experience the cold side you know. Or some people stay on the left and never look or deal with the right, or the opposite. So I lately have been just doing different things, even like getting up on different sides of the bed. You know normally I would sleep on a certain side, let me try the other side. And I did it and sometimes, wow, I could have been doing this 40 years ago, you know this is the better side for me. So all of that just lately I’ve been doing it. And especially in my playing. You know I was breathing a certain way, I was taught to breathe that way and that’s the way I breathe. You know like you were taught to ride a bike a certain way and that’s the © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

way you ride it, right? But lately I started to change the method that I breathe. And we would call it diaphragmatic breathing and they call it clavicle or chest breathing. So I never used the chest breathing much you know, and then I said let me try the chest breathing, and it works better for me. Because the muscles, I mean the air is here, in the lungs. One here and one there. So if I push pressure from the chest rather than from the bottom part of my lungs, the top part of my lungs, things come out better. And it’s just a simple little thing like that, all these years.
